docs.title: AI Assistants and Agent Skills
docs.text: AI coding assistants are trained on older code, so they tend to suggest APIs this library has removed. pydantic-schemaforms ships its own instructions for them, inside the package, so they always match the version you have installed.

docs.title: Agent skills (recommended)
docs.text:
The package includes five Agent Skills. Install them into your project with library-skills:

uvx library-skills --claude

It finds the skills in your installed packages and links them into .agents/skills/, and into .claude/skills/ with --claude (Claude Code reads only that folder). The links point into the installed package, so upgrading pydantic-schemaforms updates the skills too; run the command again after adding or removing packages. On Windows without symlink permission, add --copy.

Skill Your assistant uses it when you… pydantic-schemaforms build or change forms: fields, validation, nested forms, layouts, CSV import tables, live validation, CSRF, styling, or a form that misbehaves schemaforms-create ask for a new form from a description: "create a login form", "create a tabbed layout for a customer profile". The code comes commented like a tutorial. schemaforms-convert turn a Pydantic model, dataclass, JSON Schema, WTForms or Django form into a FormModel schemaforms-upgrade upgrade code that uses removed APIs such as FormBuilder or TabbedLayout schemaforms-document document the app's forms: docstrings and help text in the code, and a Markdown page describing every form

In Claude Code you can also call one directly, for example /schemaforms-create a contact form.

docs.title: Single-file instructions
docs.text:
For assistants that don't read skills, the same guidance is available as one file to put in your repository:

python -m pydantic_schemaforms.ai_instructions claude --write     # writes ./CLAUDE.md
python -m pydantic_schemaforms.ai_instructions copilot --write    # writes ./.github/copilot-instructions.md
python -m pydantic_schemaforms.ai_instructions generic > AI_INSTRUCTIONS.md

The file holds the shared rules, everything in the pydantic-schemaforms skill and its references, and the convert and upgrade skills. Unlike the skills, a copied file doesn't update with the package: write it again after upgrading.

usage: python -m pydantic_schemaforms.ai_instructions [-h] [--write]
                                                       [--output PATH]
                                                       [profile]

positional arguments:
  profile        Instruction profile (aliases accepted). One of: claude,
                 copilot, generic.

options:
  -h, --help     show this help message and exit
  --write        Write to the suggested destination file (e.g. CLAUDE.md)
                 instead of stdout.
  --output PATH  Write to an explicit path instead of stdout or the suggested
                 destination.

The same text is available from Python:

from pydantic_schemaforms import (
    available_instruction_profiles,
    get_app_instructions,
    suggested_instruction_filename,
)

available_instruction_profiles()           # ('claude', 'copilot', 'generic')
suggested_instruction_filename('copilot')  # '.github/copilot-instructions.md'
get_app_instructions('claude')             # the full text

Aliases such as 'github-copilot' and 'anthropic-claude' are accepted; an unknown profile raises ValueError.

docs.title: What the instructions cover
docs.text:
• The rules that matter most: import only from the top-level package, use the built-in inputs and composites instead of hand-written HTML or JavaScript, put limits in Field() constraints (not ui_options), and build HTML around submitted data with html(t'...').
  • The route pattern (render_form_html(), validate(), render_with_errors()) for FastAPI and Flask, taken from the tested examples in these docs.
  • Every ui_element, every ui_options key and every Field() setting.
  • Nested, optional and repeating sub-forms, layouts and the wizard; rule-based and live HTMX validation; data tables; CSRF, captcha, honeypot and uploads; JSON APIs; extending the library.
  • Mapping tables for converting from Pydantic, WTForms, Django and JSON Schema, and upgrade tables for every removed API.

docs.title: Try it in the example app
docs.text: The FastAPI example app renders all three single-file profiles at /ai-instructions.

docs.title: Maintaining the instructions
docs.text:
Everything shipped is generated; never edit it directly:

Generated Source pydantic_schemaforms/.agents/skills/<name>/ ai/skills/<name>/ pydantic_schemaforms/assets/ai/*_app_instructions.md ai/profiles/<profile>.md, ai/_shared.md and ai/skills/

Edit the sources, then run make ai-instructions (scripts/build_ai_instructions.py). In the sources, <!-- INCLUDE: _shared.md --> inserts the rules every skill shares, and <!-- INCLUDE-CODE: docs_src/... --> inserts an example file from docs_src/, which tests/test_docs_examples.py runs, so the skills' examples can't go stale.

tests/test_ai_skills.py checks that each skill has a valid name and description, stays under 500 lines, links only to files that exist, imports only from the top-level package, and matches its sources. It also checks that every value in the ui_element table is a registered input. The "Agent skills install from the wheel" CI job builds the wheel and installs the skills with the real library-skills CLI.

docs.title: Assets and Self-Contained Forms
docs.text:
pydantic-schemaforms is offline-by-default: by default, rendered HTML ships all required JS/CSS from this library (vendored assets are embedded/packaged).

This page documents the standard knobs used across entry points to control asset injection.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
• Vendored assets: Third-party JS/CSS copied into this repo under pydantic_schemaforms/assets/vendor/**.
  • Pinned: Versions are recorded in pydantic_schemaforms/assets/vendor/vendor_manifest.json along with sha256 checksums and source URLs.
  • asset_mode: How a renderer should include assets.

docs.title: asset_mode values
docs.text:
Most APIs accept asset_mode with these values:

  • "vendored" (default)
  • No external network required.

  • Assets are inlined (e.g., <script>…</script> / <style>…</style>) from the packaged vendor files.

  • "cdn" (explicit opt-in)

  • Emits <script src="…"> / <link href="…"> tags pointing at a CDN.

  • URLs are pinned to the versions in the vendored manifest.

  • "none"

  • Emits no assets.
  • Useful when your host app provides its own asset pipeline.

docs.title: render_form_html() — the standard entry point
docs.text:
Import from the top-level package:

from pydantic_schemaforms import render_form_html

html = render_form_html(
    MyForm,
    submit_url='/submit',
    framework='bootstrap',
    asset_mode='vendored',
    include_framework_assets=True,  # inline Bootstrap CSS/JS for self-contained HTML
)

HTMX and IMask are not injected by render_form_html(). Load them from your host page; to serve the library's vendored copies (no CDN), expose them with read_asset_text():

from fastapi import FastAPI, Response

from pydantic_schemaforms import read_asset_text

app = FastAPI()


@app.get('/vendor/htmx.min.js')
async def vendor_htmx():
    return Response(read_asset_text('assets/vendor/htmx/htmx.min.js'), media_type='application/javascript')


@app.get('/vendor/imask.min.js')
async def vendor_imask():
    return Response(read_asset_text('assets/vendor/imask/imask.min.js'), media_type='application/javascript')

Then add <script src="/vendor/htmx.min.js"></script> (and the IMask one, if you use masked inputs) to your base template.

If you already provide Bootstrap/Materialize in your host app, keep include_framework_assets=False. Use self_contained=True as a shorthand for include_framework_assets=True, asset_mode="vendored" — for Bootstrap this also embeds Bootstrap Icons as a data URI (truly zero external dependencies).

docs.title: EnhancedFormRenderer — direct renderer instance
docs.text:
Use this when you want to render multiple forms with the same configuration, or when you need finer control over the rendering pipeline.

from pydantic_schemaforms import EnhancedFormRenderer

renderer = EnhancedFormRenderer(
    framework='bootstrap',
    include_framework_assets=True,
    asset_mode='vendored',
)
html = renderer.render_form_from_model(MyForm, submit_url='/submit')

docs.title: What’s currently vendored
docs.text:
Asset Files HTMX htmx.min.js IMask imask.min.js Bootstrap bootstrap.min.css, bootstrap.bundle.min.js Bootstrap Icons bootstrap-icons.min.css, bootstrap-icons.woff2 Materialize materialize.min.css, materialize.min.js

See pydantic_schemaforms/assets/vendor/vendor_manifest.json for exact versions, SHA256 checksums, and source URLs.

docs.title: Bootstrap Icons
docs.text:
Bootstrap Icons are included as part of the Bootstrap theme’s asset delivery. The library emits <i class="bi bi-*"> elements for icons (password-toggle, field icons, etc.), so the icon font must be present for those elements to render correctly.

When include_framework_assets=True (or self_contained=True):

The CSS is inlined as a <style> block with the bootstrap-icons.woff2 font embedded as a data:font/woff2;base64,… URI. No network request is made — the icon font is fully self-contained in the HTML.

When include_framework_assets=False (default):

Bootstrap Icons are not injected by the library. Your host page is responsible for providing them. Options:

  • Use the library’s vendor endpoint (recommended for apps built on this library):
# In your FastAPI/Flask app
from pydantic_schemaforms import bootstrap_icons_css_content


@app.get('/vendor/bootstrap-icons.css')
async def bootstrap_icons():
    return Response(content=bootstrap_icons_css_content(), media_type='text/css')

Then in your base template:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="/vendor/bootstrap-icons.css" />

  • CDN (when asset_mode="cdn" and include_framework_assets=True): the library emits a pinned <link> to jsDelivr.

  • Your own asset pipeline: import bootstrap-icons from npm and bundle it yourself.

docs.title: Runtime API
docs.text:
from pydantic_schemaforms import (
    bootstrap_icons_css_tag,  # returns <style>…</style> / <link …/> / ""
    bootstrap_icons_css_content,  # returns raw CSS string with woff2 embedded
)

# Inline vendored CSS (default)
tag = bootstrap_icons_css_tag(asset_mode='vendored')

# Pinned CDN link
tag = bootstrap_icons_css_tag(asset_mode='cdn')

# Nothing (you manage the asset yourself)
tag = bootstrap_icons_css_tag(asset_mode='none')

# Raw CSS for serving via your own HTTP endpoint
css = bootstrap_icons_css_content()

docs.title: Updating vendored assets
docs.text:
Vendored updates are scripted and checksum-verified.

  • Verify vendored checksums:

  • make vendor-verify

  • Update assets:

  • make vendor-update-htmx HTMX_VERSION=…
  • make vendor-update-imask IMASK_VERSION=… (or omit to use npm latest)
  • make vendor-update-bootstrap BOOTSTRAP_VERSION=…
  • make vendor-update-bootstrap-icons BOOTSTRAP_ICONS_VERSION=…
  • make vendor-update-materialize MATERIALIZE_VERSION=…

After updating, run make vendor-verify and the test suite.

docs.title: Security note
docs.text: asset_mode="cdn" is intentionally available, but it re-introduces an external dependency at runtime. For production systems with strict supply-chain or offline requirements, prefer asset_mode="vendored".

docs.title: Data Tables (CSV Import)
docs.text:
DataTableLayout is a FormModel whose fields describe table columns instead of one instance's inputs: fields declared with Field(..., input_type=...) render as real, editable widgets per cell (a dropdown for an Enum, etc.); plain fields render as read-only, formatted text. The table is progressively enhanced client-side by a vendored copy of DataTables.js (MIT-licensed, no jQuery required) for search/sort/paging, plus optional csv/copy export buttons. Since CSV import is what this class is for, model_config["csv_upload"] defaults to True: the rendered table already comes with a file input and "Load CSV"/"Submit" buttons built in — nobody declares a separate file field or hand-builds that markup.

from enum import Enum
from pydantic_schemaforms import DataTableLayout
from pydantic_schemaforms import Field

class Color(str, Enum):
    red = "red"
    blue = "blue"
    green = "green"

class ContactImport(DataTableLayout):
    name: str
    address: str
    favorite_color: Color = Field(Color.red, input_type="select")

    model_config = {"buttons": ["csv", "copy"], "search": True, "csv_template": True}

It is not rendered on its own — it's embedded as one layout field on a plain FormModel (see Plugin Hooks), and rendered through the same render_form_html_async() call every other form in this library uses. That embedding FormModel needs nothing but the one field:

from typing import Any
from pydantic_schemaforms import render_form_html_async
from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel

class ContactsPage(FormModel):
    rows: Any = Field(
        default_factory=dict, title="Contacts",
        input_type="layout", layout_handler="datatable",
    )

html = await render_form_html_async(
    ContactsPage,
    form_data={"rows": ContactImport.as_layout_value(rows=current_rows, row_errors=row_errors)},
    submit_url="/contacts/import",
    include_submit_button=False,  # ContactImport renders its own Submit -- see below
)

layout_handler="datatable" is registered automatically the moment you import anything from pydantic_schemaforms.datatable_layout — no manual registration step needed. The embedding FormModel's framework (bootstrap/material/none), debug, and show_timing all apply to the table automatically — there's nothing DataTableLayout-specific to configure for those; they're just render_form_html_async()'s own parameters, same as any other form.

docs.title: Why include_submit_button=False?
docs.text:
Because csv_upload is on, ContactImport's own rendered output already includes a "Submit" button right below the table — pass include_submit_button=False so the embedding form doesn't also render its own generic one, which would leave two redundant "Submit"-ish controls on the page. This is safe without a nested <form>: a <button type="submit">/<input type="file"> living inside this field's own slot still submits/attaches to whatever <form> the embedding FormModel opened — only a <form> nested inside another <form> is silently dropped by the browser's HTML parser, and DataTableLayout never renders one of its own (calling ContactImport.render_form() directly raises NotImplementedError, inherited from CompositeLayoutModel — see Plugin Hooks if you're building a similar composite of your own).

If you don't want the built-in upload UI at all (e.g. a read-only display table, or your own custom upload flow), set "csv_upload": False in model_config — the embedding form's own default submit button then becomes "Submit" for the table's own editable cells, exactly like any other layout field.

docs.title: Load, review, then Submit — don't commit a CSV on one click
docs.text:
A single submit button that immediately saves whatever CSV you chose gives you no chance to catch and fix bad rows (a typo'd address, an invalid color) before they land in your database. So the built-in UI is two buttons: "Load CSV" parses the chosen file and re-renders the table with those rows for review — validation errors show up highlighted, nothing is saved yet — and "Submit" saves whatever the table is currently showing.

handle_import_post() on the model itself replaces hand-rolled load-vs-submit branching: it reads which button was clicked, parses accordingly (parse_csv_rows() for "Load", parse_submitted_rows() for "Submit" — the same default a plain fallback submit uses, so nothing is silently ignored), and returns an ImportResult with rows/row_errors already merged back into their original order (merge_rows() — an invalid row keeps its raw, as-typed values instead of vanishing):

form = await request.form()
result = await ContactImport.handle_import_post(form)

if result.action == "load":
    # Preview only -- nothing committed. Re-render with reviewing=True so
    # "Load CSV" relabels to "Reload CSV" and an info banner explains that.
    return render_page(rows=result.rows, row_errors=result.row_errors, reviewing=True, notice=result.notice)

save_to_database(result.rows)  # only "Submit" (result.action == "submit") ever gets here
if result.has_errors:
    return render_page(rows=result.rows, row_errors=result.row_errors)  # keep reviewing
return show_success_page(result.rows)

handle_import_post() reports what was actually submitted, with no opinion on whether an empty result is meaningful — a "submit" with zero rows and no errors (e.g. Submit clicked before any CSV was ever loaded) comes back looking like a valid, empty save. Decide for yourself whether that's acceptable for your app; if not, check not result.rows and not result.has_errors before calling save_to_database() and show a "nothing to submit" message instead.

Several tables can share one page, even in one form: each table's cells, file input and buttons are named under its own embedding field, so a "Load CSV" click on one table leaves the others alone (they report "submit" with their current rows). handle_import_post() finds its own table on its own. Only when two tables use the same row model does it need to be told which one to read, by the embedding field's name:

class TeamTransferForm(FormModel):
    leaving: Any = Field(default_factory=dict, input_type="layout", layout_handler="datatable")
    joining: Any = Field(default_factory=dict, input_type="layout", layout_handler="datatable")

form = await request.form(max_fields=200_000)
leaving = await EmployeeImport.handle_import_post(form, field="leaving")
joining = await EmployeeImport.handle_import_post(form, field="joining")

Pass include_assets=False to every table's as_layout_value() but the first, so the DataTables scripts load once. The example app's /employees/teams page runs this end to end.

Every cell renders as its own named <input> (read-only columns get a hidden one too, see below), so a submit's field count is rows times columns, not row count. Starlette/FastAPI's Request.form() rejects a request over its default max_fields=1000 with a 400 ("Too many fields") — a plain 5-column table already exceeds that at 200 rows. Size a higher max_fields to your largest expected import: await request.form(max_fields=200_000).

No server-side "staging" storage is needed to connect Load and Submit: the rows a CSV load rendered for review are already sitting in the table's own form fields (both the editable cells and the read-only cells' hidden inputs — see below), so whatever the browser submits on the next click already reflects any hand-fixes made in between.

Every read-only column also carries forward a hidden input with its current value, alongside its escaped display text — without that, a real browser submit would only include genuinely-editable cells' own inputs, and any read-only required field (like name above) would vanish from the submission and fail that row's validation on every save.

as_layout_value()'s reviewing/notice/discard_url parameters only affect the built-in upload UI: reviewing=True relabels the button and shows the info banner described above; notice= shows a one-off warning banner instead (handle_import_post() returns one in result.notice when "Load" is clicked with no file chosen); discard_url= adds a "discard and start over" link to the reviewing banner.

docs.title: model_config keys
docs.text:
Recognized by DataTableLayout (any other key is ignored — pydantic does not reject unknown model_config keys at runtime):

Key Default Meaning buttons [] Export buttons: "csv", "copy". "pdf" is accepted but raises NotImplementedError at render time (pdfmake isn't vendored yet). search True Show the DataTables search box. paging True Enable client-side paging. page_length 10 Default rows per page. Always included as a choice in the "entries per page" dropdown, even if not listed in length_menu. length_menu [10, 25, 50, 100] Choices offered in the "entries per page" dropdown. csv_template False Render a "Download CSV template" link above the table, as a data: URI built from ContactImport.csv_template_bytes() — no server route needed. csv_upload True Render the built-in file input + "Load CSV"/"Submit" buttons described above. Set False for a bare table with no upload UI (see above). editable True Whether cells declared with Field(..., input_type=...) actually render as editable widgets. Set False to force every cell read-only regardless of its own input_type — see below. style see below Table-appearance flags (dict) — see next section.

docs.title: editable: False — a bulk-replace-only table, no in-place edits
docs.text:
Set model_config["editable"] = False when the table should only ever be replaced wholesale by re-uploading a CSV — every cell renders read-only no matter what input_type a column declares, and the built-in UI drops "Submit" entirely, leaving one "Reload CSV" button that both parses and commits in a single click (handle_import_post() returns action="reload") — there's no separate review-then-Submit step to wait on when nothing in the table can be hand-corrected anyway:

class ReadOnlyImport(DataTableLayout):
    name: str
    favorite_color: Color = Field(Color.red, input_type="select")  # ignored -- always read-only

    model_config = {"editable": False}

result = await ReadOnlyImport.handle_import_post(await request.form())
# result.action is always "reload" here -- treat it the same as "submit":
save_to_database(result.rows)

Performance: every editable cell (a column declared with input_type=, with editable left at its default True) renders as a real <select>/ <input> widget, with no virtualization — row count drives DOM size directly. Past roughly 100 rows this gets noticeably slower to render, paginate, and submit than plain read-only cells (escaped text plus a lightweight hidden input for round-tripping). For imports past that size, prefer a read-only presentation — either model_config["editable"] = False if a bulk-replace-only flow fits (above), or declare the columns without input_type if you still want the normal Load-then-Submit review step, just without any cell being hand-editable.

docs.title: Table appearance (style)
docs.text:
model_config["style"] maps to Bootstrap's own table-* utility classes. It's a partial dict — any flag you omit keeps its default, so {"striped": True} alone only changes striping and leaves the rest as-is:

Style flag Default Bootstrap class added striped False table-striped bordered False table-bordered hover True table-hover compact False table-sm 
model_config = {"style": {"striped": True, "bordered": True, "compact": True}}

These are Bootstrap-specific classes: they have no visible effect under framework="none" (a deliberately bare table) and there's no dedicated Material variant yet — framework="material" currently gets the same Bootstrap-ish classes as framework="bootstrap".

docs.title: Performance: large imports
docs.text:
Note: imports over roughly 10,000 rows can feel slow. Rendering (not CSV parsing) dominates at that scale — every editable cell (any column declared with Field(..., input_type=...)) instantiates and renders its own input widget class, so cost scales with rows × editable columns, not just row count. Representative numbers from tests/test_benchmarks.py (one editable select column out of three, plain Bootstrap styling, buttons enabled), measured server-side only:

Rows parse_csv_rows table render 10 ~0.03 ms ~0.2 ms 100 ~0.3 ms ~1.9 ms 1,000 ~4 ms ~21 ms 10,000 ~45 ms ~220 ms

That's server render time alone — a 10,000-row table is also several MB of HTML, and the browser then has to parse that markup, build 10,000+ DOM rows, and hand them to DataTables for client-side sort/search/paging, which is usually the slower part in practice. Run pytest tests/test_benchmarks.py -k datatable yourself to reproduce these numbers on your own hardware/model shape.

If you regularly expect imports in this range: keep as many columns read-only (plain fields, no Field(input_type=...)) as your UI can tolerate — read-only cells are a cheap str()/escape, not a full widget render; and consider validating/importing in a background task instead of inline in the request/response cycle for the largest files.

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
A trimmed copy of examples/datatable_import_example.py. Notice how little of it is about CSV import: no file field, no button HTML, no load-or-submit branching and no merge logic. EmployeeImport and handle_import_post() do all of that.

from enum import Enum
from typing import Any

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse, Response
from pydantic import EmailStr

from pydantic_schemaforms import DataTableLayout, Field, FormModel, html, render_form_html_async


class Department(str, Enum):
    engineering = 'engineering'
    sales = 'sales'
    support = 'support'


class EmployeeImport(DataTableLayout):
    name: str = Field(..., input_type='text')
    email: EmailStr = Field(..., input_type='email')
    department: Department = Field(Department.engineering, input_type='select')

    model_config = {
        'buttons': ['csv', 'copy'],
        'page_length': 25,
        'csv_template': True,
        'style': {'striped': True, 'bordered': True},
    }


class EmployeeImportForm(FormModel):
    employees: Any = Field(
        default_factory=dict,
        title='Employees',
        input_type='layout',
        layout_handler='datatable',
    )


saved_rows: list[dict] = []  # stand-in for a database
app = FastAPI()


async def render_page(*, rows=None, row_errors=None, reviewing=False, notice='') -> str:
    table = EmployeeImport.as_layout_value(
        rows=saved_rows if rows is None else rows,
        row_errors=row_errors,
        reviewing=reviewing,
        notice=notice,
        discard_url='/employees/import',
    )
    return await render_form_html_async(
        EmployeeImportForm,
        form_data={'employees': table},
        submit_url='/employees/import',
        include_submit_button=False,  # the table has its own Submit
        include_framework_assets=True,
        asset_mode='cdn',
    )


@app.get('/employees/import', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def show_import():
    return await render_page()


@app.post('/employees/import', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def import_or_save(request: Request):
    result = await EmployeeImport.handle_import_post(await request.form(max_fields=200_000))

    if result.action == 'load':  # a CSV was loaded for review; nothing saved yet
        return await render_page(
            rows=result.rows, row_errors=result.row_errors, reviewing=True, notice=result.notice
        )
    if result.has_errors:  # keep reviewing until every row is valid
        return await render_page(rows=result.rows, row_errors=result.row_errors)

    saved_rows[:] = result.rows
    count = len(result.rows)
    return html(t'<p>Saved {count} rows.</p>')


@app.get('/employees/import/template.csv')
def download_template() -> Response:
    return Response(
        content=EmployeeImport.csv_template_bytes(),
        media_type='text/csv',
        headers={'Content-Disposition': 'attachment; filename="employees_template.csv"'},
    )

The example app's /employees/import page runs it with sample CSV files of 10 to 10,000 rows, /employees/directory shows a read-only table, and /employees/teams has two tables in one form.

docs.title: JSON API and JSON Schema
docs.text: A FormModel is a Pydantic model, so the same class can validate an HTML form and a JSON API request, with the same rules and the same error shape.

docs.title: One model, two routes
JSON Schema for other tools
docs.text:
get_pydantic_json_schema() returns the standard JSON Schema of the form, with nested sub-forms as $defs and $ref, for OpenAPI tooling, schema validators or code generators. Like as_api_model(), it leaves out the form settings. Pydantic's own options pass through:

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel


class Address(FormModel):
    street: str = Field(title='Street')
    city: str = Field(title='City')


class PersonForm(FormModel):
    name: str = Field(title='Full name', ui_autofocus=True)
    address: Address = Field(title='Address')


schema = PersonForm.get_pydantic_json_schema()
# {"$defs": {"Address": {...}}, "properties": {"address": {"$ref": "#/$defs/Address"}, ...}}

openapi_schema = PersonForm.get_pydantic_json_schema(ref_template='#/components/schemas/{model}')
get_json_schema()

FormModel.get_json_schema() returns the schema in the shape the form renderer uses internally, with the form settings included and sub-forms not resolved. Use get_pydantic_json_schema() for anything outside the library.

docs.title: Layout Primitives
docs.text:
To arrange a form's own fields, nest sub-forms and choose a layout=; see Layouts. The primitives on this page are for something else: arranging pieces of HTML you've already rendered on a page, such as two separate forms side by side.

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel, Layout, render_form_html


class LoginForm(FormModel):
    email: str = Field(title='Email', ui_element='email')
    password: str = Field(title='Password', ui_element='password')


class NewsletterForm(FormModel):
    email: str = Field(title='Email', ui_element='email')


login_html = render_form_html(LoginForm, submit_url='/login')
newsletter_html = render_form_html(NewsletterForm, submit_url='/newsletter')

page_section = Layout.create_grid(
    Layout.create_card('Sign in', login_html).render(),
    Layout.create_card('Get the newsletter', newsletter_html).render(),
    columns='2fr 1fr',
    gap='2rem',
).render()

Layout (also exported as LayoutComposer and LayoutFactory) creates each primitive; .render() returns its HTML:

Factory Primitive Arranges content as Layout.create_horizontal(*content) HorizontalLayout A row Layout.create_vertical(*content) VerticalLayout A column Layout.create_grid(*content, columns=...) GridLayout A CSS grid Layout.responsive_grid(*content) ResponsiveGridLayout A grid that wraps on small screens Layout.create_tabs([...]) TabLayout Tabs, from {"title": ..., "content": ...} items Layout.create_accordion([...]) AccordionLayout Collapsible panels Layout.create_card(title, content) CardLayout A card with a title Layout.create_modal(...) ModalLayout A modal dialog

Content is inserted as HTML

Titles are escaped, but content is placed into the page as is: the primitives are meant for HTML the library or your templates have already produced. Never pass text a user typed as content; build it with html(t"...") first, which escapes it.

docs.title: Live Validation (HTMX)
docs.text:
Live validation checks a field on the server while the user types or when they leave the field, and shows the result next to the form without a page reload. It uses HTMX: the field posts its value to a small endpoint and HTMX swaps the endpoint's answer into the page.

It's a convenience on top of normal validation, not a replacement: the submit route still calls validate(), because JavaScript can be turned off.

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
Three files: the model and its live validator, a page template, and the routes.

models.py
from pydantic import EmailStr

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel, LiveValidator


def live(field: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    """HTMX attributes that send the field to /validate/<field> as the user types."""
    return {
        'hx-post': f'/validate/{field}',
        'hx-trigger': 'blur, input delay:600ms',
        'hx-target': f'#{field}-feedback',
        'hx-swap': 'innerHTML',
    }


class ContactForm(FormModel):
    name: str = Field(title='Full name', min_length=2, ui_options=live('name'))
    email: EmailStr = Field(title='Email', ui_options=live('email'))


live_validator = LiveValidator.for_model(ContactForm, debounce_ms=600)
page.py
from models import live_validator

from pydantic_schemaforms import SafeHTML, html

VALIDATOR_SCRIPT = SafeHTML(live_validator.render_htmx_script())


def page(form_html: str) -> str:
    form = SafeHTML(form_html)  # trusted HTML from the library
    return html(t"""<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Contact</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.0/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css">
  <script src="https://unpkg.com/htmx.org@2.0.7"></script>
  {VALIDATOR_SCRIPT}
</head>
<body>
  <main class="container my-5">
    {form}
    <div id="name-feedback" aria-live="polite"></div>
    <div id="email-feedback" aria-live="polite"></div>
  </main>
</body>
</html>""")


def feedback(errors: list[str]) -> str:
    if not errors:
        return html(t'<span class="text-success">Looks good</span>')
    message = '; '.join(errors)  # may echo what the user typed: html() escapes it
    return html(t'<span class="text-danger">{message}</span>')
FastAPIFlask main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse
from models import ContactForm, live_validator
from page import feedback, page

from pydantic_schemaforms import html, render_form_html_async, validation_response_headers

app = FastAPI()


@app.get('/contact', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def show_contact():
    return page(await render_form_html_async(ContactForm, submit_url='/contact'))


@app.post('/contact', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def submit_contact(request: Request):
    result = ContactForm.validate(await request.form(), submit_url='/contact')
    if not result.is_valid:
        return page(await result.render_with_errors_async())
    name = result.data['name']
    return html(t'<p>Thanks, {name}!</p>')


@app.post('/validate/{field_name}', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def validate_field(field_name: str, request: Request):
    value = str((await request.form()).get(field_name, ''))
    result = live_validator.validate_field(field_name, value)
    return HTMLResponse(
        feedback(result.errors),
        headers=validation_response_headers(field_name, result.is_valid),
    )
main.py
from flask import Flask, request
from models import ContactForm, live_validator
from page import feedback, page

from pydantic_schemaforms import html, render_form_html, validation_response_headers

app = Flask(__name__)


@app.get('/contact')
def show_contact():
    return page(render_form_html(ContactForm, submit_url='/contact'))


@app.post('/contact')
def submit_contact():
    result = ContactForm.validate(request.form, submit_url='/contact')
    if not result.is_valid:
        return page(result.render_with_errors())
    name = result.data['name']
    return html(t'<p>Thanks, {name}!</p>')


@app.post('/validate/<field_name>')
def validate_field(field_name: str):
    value = request.form.get(field_name, '')
    result = live_validator.validate_field(field_name, value)
    return feedback(result.errors), validation_response_headers(field_name, result.is_valid)

Typing "A" in the name and pausing shows "String should have at least 2 characters"; finishing the name shows "Looks good".

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. LiveValidator.for_model(ContactForm) derives a check for every field from the model itself: its constraints, its type (EmailStr) and its @field_validators. There's nothing to keep in sync.
  2. ui_options=live("name") adds HTMX attributes to the input: post to /validate/name on blur and 600 ms after the user stops typing, and put the answer into #name-feedback. Any ui_options key that isn't a known option is written onto the input as an attribute.
  3. One endpoint serves every field. validate_field(name, value) runs that field's check and returns a result with is_valid and errors. An unknown field name is reported as valid, so a stray request never breaks the page.
  4. validation_response_headers() tells the script from render_htmx_script() the outcome, so it marks the input is-valid or is-invalid and copies the message into the input's tooltip.

The feedback is built with html(t"...") because a message can include what the user typed: email-validator's "The domain name example.con does not exist", for example. The feedback elements use aria-live="polite" so screen readers announce the result.

docs.title: Checks that aren't in the model
docs.text:
FieldValidator builds a check from rules, with your own messages. Register it after for_model() to replace that one field's check:

from pydantic_schemaforms import CustomRule, FieldValidator

username = FieldValidator("username")
username.min_length(3, message="At least 3 characters")
username.add_rule(CustomRule(
    lambda value: not value.lower().startswith("admin"),
    message="Usernames can't start with 'admin'",
))
live_validator.register_field_validator(username)

The available rules are in Validation Rules.

docs.title: Email addresses that can receive mail
docs.text:
DeliverableEmailStr is a drop-in replacement for EmailStr that also looks up the domain's mail servers (MX records), so ada@example.con is rejected with a message saying why. It works in validate() and in live validation with nothing else to set up, and needs the email extra (pydantic-schemaforms[email]).

It's a real DNS lookup, so it always runs on the server and takes a moment: keep a debounce of at least 600 ms for it, or check it on blur only with live(...) returning "hx-trigger": "blur" for that field.

docs.title: Triggers and debounce
docs.text:
for_model(..., debounce_ms=600) checks on blur and as the user types. For other combinations, pass an HTMXValidationConfig:

from pydantic_schemaforms import HTMXValidationConfig, LiveValidator

config = HTMXValidationConfig(
    validate_on_blur=True,
    validate_on_input=False,   # blur only
    validate_on_change=False,
    debounce_ms=400,
)
live_validator = LiveValidator.for_model(ContactForm, config=config)

The trigger written on the input (hx-trigger) is set by your ui_options, so keep the two in step.

docs.title: Several forms, one endpoint
docs.text: LiveValidator.for_model(ContactForm, SignupForm) covers several forms with one validator and one /validate/{field_name} route. Field names must be unique across those forms; for a repeated name, the last one registered wins.

docs.title: Styling the result
docs.text:
Bootstrap styles is-valid and is-invalid on inputs out of the box. For Material or plain HTML, add your own rule:

input.is-invalid { border-color: #dc3545; }
input.is-valid   { border-color: #198754; }
Rendering a single field by hand

live_validator.render_field_with_live_validation("email", field_type="email", label="Email") returns one labelled input with its HTMX attributes and its own feedback element, for pages where you build the markup yourself instead of rendering a whole FormModel.

The example app's /live-validation and /email-dns-validation pages run these patterns live.

docs.title: Plugin Hooks and Custom Composites
docs.text: You can add your own inputs and your own composite controls (a whole table, a repeating structure, a custom picker) without changing the library. Both are registered at startup and then used through ui_element or a layout field like any built-in one.

docs.title: Custom inputs
docs.text:
Subclass an existing input and register it under a new ui_element name:

from typing import Any

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel, TextInput, register_input_class, render_form_html


class ExtensionInput(TextInput):
    """A phone extension: up to six digits, with a numeric keypad on phones."""

    ui_element = 'extension'

    def render(self, **kwargs: Any) -> str:
        kwargs.setdefault('inputmode', 'numeric')
        kwargs.setdefault('pattern', r'\d{1,6}')
        kwargs.setdefault('maxlength', 6)
        return super().render(**kwargs)


register_input_class(ExtensionInput, aliases=('phone_extension',))


class DirectoryEntry(FormModel):
    name: str = Field(title='Name')
    extension: str = Field('', title='Extension', ui_element='extension')


form_html = render_form_html(DirectoryEntry, submit_url='/directory')

Subclassing a built-in input such as TextInput keeps everything it already does: escaping every value, the label, help text, error message and the accessibility wiring. Override render() to adjust the attributes, then hand off to super().render().

  • register_input_class(cls, aliases=(...)) registers one class, under its ui_element and any aliases.
  • register_inputs([...]) registers several at once.
  • reset_input_registry() removes the custom ones, for tests or hot reload.

Keep custom inputs to the accessibility baseline in Accessibility: inherit render_with_label() (from FormInput) rather than writing your own, so the label, help text and error get their ids and the control gets aria-invalid/aria-describedby; make sure render() passes aria-* keyword arguments through to the control (the validate_attributes() helper does this); and keep text at 4.5:1 contrast. A built-in input also needs a widget-gallery entry, which puts it under the axe-core gate in tests/playwright/test_example_pages.py.

docs.title: Registering Custom Layout Renderers
docs.text:
LayoutEngine dispatches a field to a registered custom renderer through two independent keyspaces, both backed by the same LayoutEngine._custom_renderers registry and the same LayoutRenderer callable signature — (field_name, field_schema, value, ui_info, context, engine) -> str:

  1. layout_handler keyspace — only reached when the field itself is declared input_type="layout", plus a layout_handler (or layout_renderer) name in json_schema_extra/FormField kwargs. This is the mechanism DataTableLayout uses (see below): the field's own value carries whatever the renderer needs.
  2. ui_element keyspace — reached directly by a field's own ui_element/input_type string, whatever it is, via LayoutEngine.get_renderer_for_element(ui_element). This is the mechanism model_list uses internally (FormField(..., input_type="model_list")) — from the field declaration's point of view nothing about model_list changed, but internally it's dispatched through this same registry rather than a hardcoded check, so it's a second, real, load-bearing example of this mechanism working end-to-end (not just a name-collision risk to avoid).

Use register_layout_renderer(name, renderer) for either keyspace — which one a given name lands in depends entirely on what triggers the lookup on the field side (input_type="layout" + layout_handler=name, vs. a field whose own input_type/ui_element literally equals name), not on anything about the registration call itself.

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel, LayoutEngine, SafeHTML, html, render_form_html


@LayoutEngine.layout_renderer('step_list', builtin=False)
def render_step_list(field_name, field_schema, value, ui_info, context, engine) -> str:
    items = SafeHTML(''.join(html(t'<li>{step}</li>') for step in (value or [])))
    return html(t'<ol class="step-list" data-field="{field_name}">{items}</ol>')


class OnboardingForm(FormModel):
    steps: list[str] = Field(
        ['Account', 'Billing', 'Review'],
        title='Steps',
        input_type='layout',
        layout_handler='step_list',
    )


form_html = render_form_html(OnboardingForm, submit_url='/onboarding')

The renderer builds its HTML with html(t'...'), like everything else in the library, so each step's text is escaped. The field declares input_type="layout" and names the renderer with layout_handler; its value (here the list of steps) is what the renderer receives.

  • Names are arbitrary strings; collisions overwrite the previous handler.
  • Call LayoutEngine.reset_layout_renderers() in tests to clear non-builtin state (see builtin=True below — a renderer registered that way survives this call).
  • Handlers receive the active LayoutEngine instance and the original renderer via engine._renderer if you need to reuse field rendering helpers.

docs.title: requires_multipart — declare a nested file input
docs.text:
If your renderer might emit its own <input type="file"> inside the field's own output (as DataTableLayout does when csv_upload is on), pass requires_multipart to register_layout_renderer/layout_renderer. A nested file input like that isn't a top-level FormModel field, so the form's own file-field scan — which only sees this field's layout element, not what it renders — can never discover it on its own, and the enclosing <form> would silently miss enctype="multipart/form-data", without which a browser sends only the chosen file's name, never its contents:

def _needs_multipart(value: Any) -> bool:
    # Called with this field's raw value (whatever your as_layout_value()-
    # equivalent built) at render time; return whether *that specific
    # value* needs multipart encoding.
    return bool(value) and value.get('csv_upload_enabled', False)

@LayoutEngine.layout_renderer('steps', requires_multipart=_needs_multipart)
def render_steps(field_name, field_schema, value, ui_info, context, engine):
    ...

DataTableLayout wires this to its own csv_upload config flag — see pydantic_schemaforms/rendering/datatable_renderer.py. If your composite never renders a file input, omit the parameter (the default None means "never needs multipart").

docs.title: builtin=True and the @LayoutEngine.layout_renderer decorator
docs.text:
A renderer this library ships (like DataTableLayout's or model_list's) only registers itself once per process, at import time. If you register it the plain way and something later calls LayoutEngine.reset_layout_renderers() — several test fixtures across this project's own suite do, between tests — it's gone for the rest of the process, since nothing re-imports the registering module afterward. Pass builtin=True to register_layout_renderer to mark a renderer as library-owned so resets leave it alone:

LayoutEngine.register_layout_renderer("datatable", render_datatable_layout_field, builtin=True)

Or use the decorator form, which defaults builtin=True (it's meant for exactly this "register my own reusable composite once, at import time" case):

@LayoutEngine.layout_renderer("datatable")
def render_datatable_layout_field(field_name, field_schema, value, ui_info, context, engine):
    ...

One-off, app-level, or test-only renderers should leave builtin at its default (False) so reset_layout_renderers() still clears them between tests, same as always.

docs.title: Real, working composite examples
docs.text:
Earlier versions of this guide illustrated the mechanism with a WizardForm example that was never actually shipped. Three real composites in this library demonstrate both keyspaces end-to-end:

  • DataTableLayout (pydantic_schemaforms/datatable_layout.py + pydantic_schemaforms/rendering/datatable_renderer.py) — the layout_handler keyspace. A FormModel subclass whose own fields ARE the composite's structure (table columns), embedded as input_type="layout", layout_handler="datatable". See Data Tables for the full pattern, including as_layout_value() for building the field's value.
  • model_list (pydantic_schemaforms/rendering/model_list_renderer.py) — the ui_element keyspace. FormField(..., input_type="model_list") on a list[ItemModel]-annotated field, where ItemModel is any ordinary, unmodified FormModel — there's no wrapper class at all, since the item's shape already comes from its own type annotation.
  • nested_model (pydantic_schemaforms/rendering/nested_model_renderer.py) — also the ui_element keyspace, inferred from a field typed as another FormModel. It renders the sub-form's fields under dotted input names and is how complex forms are composed (see Nested Forms and Lists).

Every registered renderer is called with six positional arguments, (field_name, field_schema, value, ui_info, context, engine). The field's own error message is context.error, and its nested errors (same shape as its value; see Nested Forms and Lists) are context.child_errors.

docs.title: CompositeLayoutModel: a base for FormModel-shaped composites
docs.text:
If your composite is shaped like DataTableLayout — a FormModel subclass whose own fields define the composite's structure, meant to be embedded as a layout field and never rendered on its own — subclass pydantic_schemaforms.composite_layout.CompositeLayoutModel instead of FormModel directly. It disables render_form() with a clear NotImplementedError pointing callers at your own value-bundling classmethod (the as_layout_value() convention DataTableLayout uses), so nobody accidentally calls it as if it rendered one instance's inputs.

Not every composite needs this base — model_list doesn't, since its item model is just an ordinary FormModel referenced via a list[ItemModel] annotation, not a class of its own that needs render_form() disabled. Reach for CompositeLayoutModel specifically when your composite's own fields ARE its structure (table columns, wizard steps, and similar).

docs.title: Packaging Tips
docs.text:
• For libraries: register your inputs/layouts in your package __init__ or an explicit setup() function that users call during startup, and pass builtin=True (or use the @LayoutEngine.layout_renderer(name) decorator) so reset_layout_renderers() calls elsewhere (e.g. in a consuming app's own test suite) don't silently remove your renderer.
  • For app code: register once at process start (e.g., FastAPI lifespan, Django AppConfig.ready). Avoid per-request registration. Leave builtin at its default (False) so your own tests can still reset cleanly between runs.
  • Keep renderers pure and side-effect free; they should return HTML strings and not mutate shared state.

docs.title: Rule-Based Validation
docs.text:
Most forms need nothing beyond the Pydantic validation in the Validation chapter. The library also has a rule-based layer, FormValidator, for three situations:

  • A ready-made check that isn't a Pydantic type, such as PhoneRule.
  • Rules you switch on or off per route without changing the model, for example a stricter check on an admin page.
  • The same rules for live validation and the submit route; see Live Validation.

Rules run on the submitted data alongside the model's own validation, and their errors are shown the same way.

docs.title: Model and rules together
Field rules
docs.text:
rules.field("phone") returns that field's rule list; add_rule() adds to it and returns it again, so rules chain:

rules.field("username").add_rule(MinLengthRule(3)).add_rule(MaxLengthRule(20))

Every rule takes an optional message= to replace its default text. The full list (RequiredRule, MinLengthRule, MaxLengthRule, EmailRule, EmailDeliverabilityRule, PhoneRule, NumericRangeRule, DateRangeRule, RegexRule, CustomRule) is in Validation Rules.

CustomRule wraps any function that returns True for a valid value:

from pydantic_schemaforms import CustomRule

rules.field("username").add_rule(
    CustomRule(lambda value: not value.lower().startswith("admin"),
               message="Usernames can't start with 'admin'")
)

docs.title: Cross-field rules
docs.text: add_cross_field_rule() takes a function that gets all the data and returns (is_valid, errors), where errors maps a field name to its message. That puts the message on the field the user has to change, like minors_need_consent above.

docs.title: Running rules on their own
docs.text:
rules.validate(data) returns (is_valid, errors) without a model, with each field's messages as a list:

is_valid, errors = rules.validate({"phone": "abc", "age": 15})
# (False, {"phone": ["Please enter a valid phone number"],
#          "parental_consent": ["A parent must agree for anyone under 18"]})
Quick standalone checks

create_email_validator() and create_password_strength_validator() return functions that check a single value and give back a ValidationResponse with is_valid, errors, and for passwords also warnings and suggestions ("Add a number (0-9)"). They're handy for an API endpoint or a live check of one field.

docs.title: Forms Built at Runtime
docs.text:
Usually a form is a class you write. When the fields are only known while the app runs, for example an admin screen where staff design a survey, or fields stored in a database, build the FormModel class with Pydantic's create_model(). The result is an ordinary FormModel: it renders, validates and re-renders errors exactly like a class you wrote.

from pydantic import create_model

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel, render_form_html

# Loaded from a database or a config file at runtime
FIELDS = [
    {'name': 'name', 'title': 'Your name', 'ui_element': 'text', 'required': True},
    {'name': 'email', 'title': 'Email', 'ui_element': 'email', 'required': True},
    {'name': 'rating', 'title': 'Rating', 'ui_element': 'rating', 'required': False},
    {'name': 'comments', 'title': 'Comments', 'ui_element': 'textarea', 'required': False},
]


def build_form(fields: list[dict]) -> type[FormModel]:
    return create_model(
        'FeedbackForm',
        __base__=FormModel,
        **{
            spec['name']: (
                str,
                Field(
                    ... if spec['required'] else '',
                    title=spec['title'],
                    ui_element=spec['ui_element'],
                ),
            )
            for spec in fields
        },
    )


FeedbackForm = build_form(FIELDS)
form_html = render_form_html(FeedbackForm, submit_url='/feedback')
  • __base__=FormModel makes the new class a form.
  • Each field is a (type, Field(...)) pair, with the same Field() settings as anywhere else: title, ui_element, constraints, ui_options.
  • ... as the default makes a field required.
  • Build each class once, when the definition changes, rather than on every request: Pydantic does real work to create a model.

Treat stored field definitions as untrusted input if users can edit them: choose the type and ui_element from a list you control, rather than passing stored strings straight through.

Coming: JSON Schema import

Building a form straight from a JSON Schema document is planned (#235). Until then, create_model() is the way to build a form at runtime.

docs.title: Render Timing and Logging
docs.text: Two development aids: how long a form took to render, and the library's log messages.

docs.title: Render timing
docs.text: Use render timing options to inspect form performance during development.

docs.title: Timing behavior
docs.text:
The renderer measures render duration internally and can expose it in two ways:

  1. Inline timing text in form output (show_timing=True)
  2. Debug panel timing metadata (debug=True)

docs.title: Inline timing (show_timing=True)
docs.text:
from pydantic_schemaforms import render_form_html

html = render_form_html(
    MyForm,
    submit_url="/submit",
    show_timing=True,
)

This adds a small timing indicator in the rendered form markup.

docs.title: Debug panel (debug=True)
docs.text:
html = render_form_html(
    MyForm,
    submit_url="/submit",
    debug=True,
)

This appends a richer debug panel that includes timing plus schema/render metadata.

docs.title: Combined usage
docs.text:
html = render_form_html(
    MyForm,
    submit_url="/submit",
    show_timing=True,
    debug=True,
)

Use this combination for local diagnosis of slow forms.

docs.title: Async usage
docs.text:
The same options are available in async mode:

from pydantic_schemaforms import render_form_html_async

html = await render_form_html_async(
    MyForm,
    submit_url="/submit",
    show_timing=True,
)

docs.title: With logging
docs.text:
If you also want log output, enable it explicitly:

html = render_form_html(
    MyForm,
    submit_url="/submit",
    show_timing=True,
    enable_logging=True,
)

enable_logging=True controls debug log emission and is independent of timing display in HTML.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Keep show_timing=False and debug=False for production-facing pages.
  • Use representative data when benchmarking complex forms (nested models, model lists, layout-heavy schemas).

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: pydantic-schemaforms uses Python's standard logging module and keeps detailed renderer logs opt-in.

docs.title: What is logged by default
docs.text:
Default behavior for rendering calls:

  • No per-render debug/timing log lines are emitted.
  • Form rendering still works normally with no logging setup.

This keeps production output quiet unless you opt in.

docs.title: Enabling renderer logs
docs.text:
Use enable_logging=True on render calls:

from pydantic_schemaforms import render_form_html

html = render_form_html(
    MyForm,
    submit_url="/submit",
    enable_logging=True,
)

When enabled, the renderer emits debug lines such as render duration and model name.

docs.title: Logging level configuration
docs.text:
Renderer logs are emitted at DEBUG level. Configure logging accordingly:

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)

If your app is set to INFO/WARNING, DEBUG lines will remain hidden.

docs.title: Per-request debugging pattern
docs.text:
For web apps, conditionally enable logs during troubleshooting:

from fastapi import FastAPI, Query
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse
from pydantic_schemaforms import render_form_html

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/demo", response_class=HTMLResponse)
def demo(debug_logs: bool = Query(False)):
    form_html = render_form_html(
        MyForm,
        submit_url="/demo",
        enable_logging=debug_logs,
    )
    return f"<html><body>{form_html}</body></html>"

docs.title: Related options
docs.text:
• show_timing=True: displays render timing in the returned HTML.
  • debug=True: appends the renderer debug panel to returned HTML.
  • enable_logging=True: emits renderer debug log lines.

These options are independent and can be combined.

docs.title: Security guidance
docs.text:
• Avoid logging raw secrets (CSRF tokens, passwords, session IDs).
  • Prefer logging outcomes and context (route, request_id, user_id) over sensitive payload values.

Complete forms for common jobs. Each one is a working app: copy the model and the routes, run it, and change what you need. They assume you've read the Tutorial; each recipe explains only what is new.

docs.title: Shipping and Billing Addresses
docs.text:
One Address model, used for both the shipping and the billing address. The billing address is optional: it's only needed when it differs.

models.py
from typing import Literal, Self

from pydantic import EmailStr, model_validator

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel


class Address(FormModel):
    street: str = Field(title='Street')
    city: str = Field(title='City', min_length=2)
    postal_code: str = Field(title='Postal code', pattern=r'^[A-Za-z0-9 -]{3,10}$')
    country: Literal['US', 'CA', 'GB', 'FR', 'DE'] = Field('US', title='Country')


class CheckoutForm(FormModel):
    email: EmailStr = Field(title='Email for the receipt')
    shipping: Address = Field(title='Shipping address')
    billing_same_as_shipping: bool = Field(True, title='Bill to the shipping address')
    billing: Address | None = Field(None, title='Billing address', ui_collapsed=True)

    @model_validator(mode='after')
    def billing_given(self) -> Self:
        if not self.billing_same_as_shipping and self.billing is None:
            raise ValueError('Enter a billing address, or bill to the shipping address')
        return self

    def billing_address(self) -> Address:
        return self.shipping if self.billing_same_as_shipping else self.billing
FastAPIFlask main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse
from models import CheckoutForm

from pydantic_schemaforms import html, render_form_html_async

app = FastAPI()
FORM_OPTIONS = {'submit_url': '/checkout', 'include_framework_assets': True, 'asset_mode': 'cdn'}


@app.get('/checkout', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def show_checkout():
    return await render_form_html_async(CheckoutForm, **FORM_OPTIONS)


@app.post('/checkout', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def checkout(request: Request):
    result = CheckoutForm.validate(await request.form(), **FORM_OPTIONS)
    if not result.is_valid:
        return await result.render_with_errors_async()
    billing = result.instance.billing_address()
    return html(t'<p>Billing {billing.street}, {billing.city}.</p>')

    if not result.is_valid:

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The same model, twice. Each field gets its own section with its own inputs (shipping.city, billing.city), and errors are reported under the right one.
  • billing: Address | None is an optional sub-form. Its inputs aren't required in the browser, and when it comes back blank (or still at its defaults, such as the country), validate() returns None for it. As soon as the user fills in part of it, the whole sub-form is checked.
  • ui_collapsed=True starts the billing section folded away. It opens by itself when it contains an error.
  • The model validator asks for a billing address only when the box is unticked, and its message is shown at the top of the form.
  • result.instance is the validated CheckoutForm object, so the route can call billing_address() on it.

docs.title: Contact Form
docs.text:
A contact form with a topic, a message and a hidden trap for spam bots.

models.py
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import EmailStr

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel


class ContactForm(FormModel):
    name: str = Field(title='Your name', min_length=2, ui_autofocus=True)
    email: EmailStr = Field(title='Email')
    topic: Literal['Question', 'Feedback', 'Bug report'] = Field('Question', title='Topic')
    message: str = Field(title='Message', min_length=10, max_length=2000, ui_element='textarea')
    website: str = Field('', ui_element='honeypot')  # hidden; only bots fill it in

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• topic: Literal[...] becomes a dropdown of the three topics, with "Question" selected by default.
  • max_length=2000 on the message limits it in the browser and on the server.
  • ui_element="honeypot" renders a text box that people can't see or tab to, but bots that fill in every input will. When it comes back filled in, the route answers as if the message was sent and drops it, so the bot learns nothing.

A honeypot stops simple bots. For more, add a captcha field; see Input Types.

docs.title: Edit Form from a Database Row
docs.text:
Show a saved record in a form, let the user change it, and save it back.

models.py
from datetime import date
from enum import Enum

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel


class Status(str, Enum):
    draft = 'draft'
    active = 'active'
    archived = 'archived'


class ProductForm(FormModel):
    name: str = Field(title='Name', min_length=2)
    price: float = Field(title='Price', ge=0)
    status: Status = Field(Status.draft, title='Status')
    launch_date: date | None = Field(None, title='Launch date')
    featured: bool = Field(False, title='Featured on the home page')


PRODUCTS = {  # stands in for your database
    1: {
        'id': 1,
        'name': 'Desk lamp',
        'price': 39.5,
        'status': Status.active,
        'launch_date': date(2026, 3, 1),
        'featured': True,
        'created_by': 'ada',
    },
}
FastAPIFlask main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Request
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse, RedirectResponse
from models import PRODUCTS, ProductForm

from pydantic_schemaforms import render_form_html_async

app = FastAPI()
ASSETS = {'include_framework_assets': True, 'asset_mode': 'cdn'}


def load_product(product_id: int) -> dict:
    if product_id not in PRODUCTS:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404)
    return PRODUCTS[product_id]


@app.get('/products/{product_id}/edit', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def edit_product(product_id: int):
    row = load_product(product_id)
    return await render_form_html_async(
        ProductForm,
        form_data={name: row[name] for name in ProductForm.model_fields},
        submit_url=f'/products/{product_id}/edit',
        **ASSETS,
    )


@app.post('/products/{product_id}/edit', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def save_product(product_id: int, request: Request):
    row = load_product(product_id)
    result = ProductForm.validate(
        await request.form(), submit_url=f'/products/{product_id}/edit', **ASSETS
    )
    if not result.is_valid:
        return await result.render_with_errors_async()
    row.update(result.data)
    return RedirectResponse(f'/products/{product_id}/edit', status_code=303)
main.py
from flask import Flask, abort, redirect, request
from models import PRODUCTS, ProductForm

from pydantic_schemaforms import render_form_html

app = Flask(__name__)
ASSETS = {'include_framework_assets': True, 'asset_mode': 'cdn'}


def load_product(product_id: int) -> dict:
    if product_id not in PRODUCTS:
        abort(404)
    return PRODUCTS[product_id]


@app.get('/products/<int:product_id>/edit')
def edit_product(product_id: int):
    row = load_product(product_id)
    return render_form_html(
        ProductForm,
        form_data={name: row[name] for name in ProductForm.model_fields},
        submit_url=f'/products/{product_id}/edit',
        **ASSETS,
    )


@app.post('/products/<int:product_id>/edit')
def save_product(product_id: int):
    row = load_product(product_id)
    result = ProductForm.validate(request.form, submit_url=f'/products/{product_id}/edit', **ASSETS)
    if not result.is_valid:
        return result.render_with_errors()
    row.update(result.data)
    return redirect(f'/products/{product_id}/edit', code=303)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• form_data= fills the form. Pass the row's values as they are: dates, Enum members and numbers are shown correctly, so there's nothing to convert.
  • Only the form's fields are passed. The row also has id and created_by, which the user must not edit. They are left out of form_data, and since they aren't fields of ProductForm, a request that sends them anyway can't change them: validate() ignores unknown keys.
  • result.data has the same keys as the model, typed (Status.archived, date(2026, 3, 1), None for a cleared date), ready to write back.

If your rows are ORM objects or Pydantic models, build the dictionary the same way: {name: getattr(row, name) for name in ProductForm.model_fields}.

docs.title: File Upload
docs.text:
A form with a file. The library renders the file input (with drag and drop) and sends the form as multipart/form-data; your route checks and stores the file.

models.py
from typing import Any

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel


class UploadForm(FormModel):
    title: str = Field(title='Title', min_length=2)
    document: Any = Field(
        None,
        title='Document',
        description='PDF or Word, up to 5 MB.',
        ui_element='file',
        ui_options={'accept': '.pdf,.docx'},
    )


ALLOWED_TYPES = {'.pdf', '.docx'}
MAX_BYTES = 5 * 1024 * 1024
FastAPIFlask main.py
from pathlib import Path

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse
from models import ALLOWED_TYPES, MAX_BYTES, UploadForm
from starlette.datastructures import UploadFile

from pydantic_schemaforms import html, render_form_html_async

app = FastAPI()
FORM_OPTIONS = {'submit_url': '/upload', 'include_framework_assets': True, 'asset_mode': 'cdn'}


def check_upload(upload: object) -> tuple[str | None, bytes]:
    if not isinstance(upload, UploadFile) or not upload.filename:
        return 'Choose a file to upload', b''
    if Path(upload.filename).suffix.lower() not in ALLOWED_TYPES:
        return 'Upload a PDF or Word document', b''
    content = upload.file.read(MAX_BYTES + 1)
    if len(content) > MAX_BYTES:
        return 'The file is larger than 5 MB', b''
    return None, content


@app.get('/upload', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def show_upload():
    return await render_form_html_async(UploadForm, **FORM_OPTIONS)


@app.post('/upload', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def upload(request: Request):
    form = await request.form()
    result = UploadForm.validate(form, **FORM_OPTIONS)
    file_error, content = check_upload(form.get('document'))
    if not result.is_valid or file_error:
        errors = {**result.errors, **({'document': file_error} if file_error else {})}
        return await render_form_html_async(
            UploadForm, form_data={'title': form.get('title')}, errors=errors, **FORM_OPTIONS
        )
    size = len(content)
    return html(t'<p>Stored "{result.data["title"]}" ({size} bytes).</p>')
main.py
from pathlib import Path

from flask import Flask, request
from models import ALLOWED_TYPES, MAX_BYTES, UploadForm
from werkzeug.datastructures import CombinedMultiDict, FileStorage

from pydantic_schemaforms import html, render_form_html

app = Flask(__name__)
app.config['MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH'] = MAX_BYTES + 64 * 1024  # Flask refuses bigger requests
FORM_OPTIONS = {'submit_url': '/upload', 'include_framework_assets': True, 'asset_mode': 'cdn'}


def check_upload(upload: object) -> tuple[str | None, bytes]:
    if not isinstance(upload, FileStorage) or not upload.filename:
        return 'Choose a file to upload', b''
    if Path(upload.filename).suffix.lower() not in ALLOWED_TYPES:
        return 'Upload a PDF or Word document', b''
    content = upload.stream.read(MAX_BYTES + 1)
    if len(content) > MAX_BYTES:
        return 'The file is larger than 5 MB', b''
    return None, content


@app.get('/upload')
def show_upload():
    return render_form_html(UploadForm, **FORM_OPTIONS)


@app.post('/upload')
def upload():
    result = UploadForm.validate(CombinedMultiDict([request.form, request.files]), **FORM_OPTIONS)
    file_error, content = check_upload(request.files.get('document'))
    if not result.is_valid or file_error:
        errors = {**result.errors, **({'document': file_error} if file_error else {})}
        return render_form_html(
            UploadForm,
            form_data={'title': request.form.get('title')},
            errors=errors,
            **FORM_OPTIONS,
        )
    size = len(content)
    return html(t'<p>Stored "{result.data["title"]}" ({size} bytes).</p>')

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• ui_element="file" renders the file input. accept limits what the file picker offers; multiple=True would allow several files. A form with a file input gets enctype="multipart/form-data" by itself.
  • The field is typed Any, because the uploaded file arrives as your framework's own object: Starlette's UploadFile or Werkzeug's FileStorage. Flask keeps files apart from the other fields, so the route combines request.form and request.files before validating.
  • check_upload() checks the file itself: that one was chosen, its extension, and its size, reading at most one byte more than the limit. Its message is added to the form's errors so it shows under the file input.
  • The browser can't keep a chosen file across a re-render, so after an error the user picks it again. The title is kept.

Treat uploads as untrusted

accept and the file name are only hints: check the content before you use it, store files outside your web root under names you generate, and never show a file name in HTML without escaping it (html(t"...") does).

FastAPIFlask main.py
from pathlib import Path

from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse
from fastapi.templating import Jinja2Templates

docs.title: Login and Registration
docs.text:
A login form and a registration form, with the checks that only your app can make (is the password right? is the username free?) shown in the form like any other error.

models.py
from pydantic import EmailStr, ValidationInfo, field_validator

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel


class LoginForm(FormModel):
    username: str = Field(title='Username', ui_autofocus=True)
    password: str = Field(title='Password', ui_element='password')
    remember_me: bool = Field(False, title='Keep me signed in')


class RegistrationForm(FormModel):
    username: str = Field(
        title='Username',
        min_length=3,
        max_length=30,
        pattern=r'^[a-z0-9_]+$',
        description='Lowercase letters, numbers and underscores.',
    )
    email: EmailStr = Field(title='Email')
    password: str = Field(title='Password', ui_element='password', min_length=12)
    confirm_password: str = Field(title='Confirm password', ui_element='password')
    accept_terms: bool = Field(False, title='I accept the terms of service', validate_default=True)

    @field_validator('username', mode='before')
    @classmethod
    def normalize_username(cls, value: str) -> str:
        return value.strip().lower()

    @field_validator('confirm_password')
    @classmethod
    def passwords_match(cls, value: str, info: ValidationInfo) -> str:
        if value != info.data.get('password'):
            raise ValueError('Passwords do not match')
        return value

    @field_validator('accept_terms')
    @classmethod
    def terms_accepted(cls, value: bool) -> bool:
        if not value:
            raise ValueError('You must accept the terms to create an account')
        return value

from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse, RedirectResponse
from models import LoginForm, RegistrationForm

from pydantic_schemaforms import render_form_html_async

app = FastAPI()
ASSETS = {'include_framework_assets': True, 'asset_mode': 'cdn'}


def authenticate(username: str, password: str) -> bool:
    return False  # look the user up and verify the password hash


def username_taken(username: str) -> bool:
    return username == 'admin'


def create_user(data: dict) -> None: ...  # hash the password, then store the user


@app.get('/login', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def show_login():
    return await render_form_html_async(LoginForm, submit_url='/login', **ASSETS)


@app.post('/login', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def login(request: Request):
    result = LoginForm.validate(await request.form(), submit_url='/login', **ASSETS)
    if not result.is_valid:
        return await result.render_with_errors_async()
    if not authenticate(result.data['username'], result.data['password']):
        return await render_form_html_async(
            LoginForm,
            form_data={'username': result.data['username']},
            errors={'_errors': 'Wrong username or password'},
            submit_url='/login',
            **ASSETS,
        )
    return RedirectResponse('/', status_code=303)


@app.get('/register', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def show_register():
    return await render_form_html_async(RegistrationForm, submit_url='/register', **ASSETS)


@app.post('/register', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def register(request: Request):
    form = await request.form()
    result = RegistrationForm.validate(form, submit_url='/register', **ASSETS)
    if not result.is_valid:
        return await result.render_with_errors_async()
    if username_taken(result.data['username']):
        return await render_form_html_async(
            RegistrationForm,
            form_data=dict(form),
            errors={'username': 'That username is taken'},
            submit_url='/register',
            **ASSETS,
        )
    create_user(result.data)
    return RedirectResponse('/login', status_code=303)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The confirmation must match. passwords_match reads the password from info.data and puts its error under the confirmation field.
  • The terms box must be ticked. validate_default=True makes Pydantic run terms_accepted even when the box is left unticked (and so not submitted), so the user sees your message instead of nothing.
  • The username is cleaned up first. mode="before" lowercases and trims it before pattern checks it.
  • Errors from your own checks go through render_form_html()'s errors=: {"username": "..."} shows under that field, and "_errors" shows a message for the whole form in the summary at the top. Pass form_data= so the user's input stays filled in. The login form only puts back the username, never the password.
  • After success, redirect (303) so reloading the page doesn't send the form again.

Before going live

Store password hashes, never passwords (use a library such as argon2-cffi or bcrypt). Protect both forms with a CSRF token once users are logged in; see CSRF Protection.

docs.title: Order with Line Items
docs.text:
An order with any number of lines, each with a product, a quantity and a unit price, and a total worked out on the server.

models.py
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal

from pydantic import computed_field

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel


class LineItem(FormModel):
    product: str = Field(title='Product', min_length=2)
    quantity: int = Field(1, title='Quantity', ge=1, le=999)
    unit_price: Decimal = Field(title='Unit price', ge=0, decimal_places=2, ui_element='currency')

    @computed_field
    @property
    def total(self) -> Decimal:
        return self.quantity * self.unit_price


class OrderForm(FormModel):
    customer: str = Field(title='Customer', ui_autofocus=True)
    delivery_date: date = Field(title='Delivery date')
    items: list[LineItem] = Field(
        default_factory=list,
        title='Line items',
        min_length=1,
        max_length=50,
        ui_add_button_label='Add a line',
        ui_item_title_template='{product}',
    )
    notes: str = Field('', title='Notes', ui_element='textarea')

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• list[LineItem] is a repeating sub-form with an "Add a line" button. min_length=1 means the form starts with one empty line and can't be sent with none; max_length=50 caps it.
  • ui_item_title_template="{product}" titles each line's card with its product as the user types it.

docs.title: Settings with a Code Field
docs.text:
A settings form where part of the settings is JSON, TOML or a script, typed into a text area with syntax highlighting and a Format button, and checked on the server.

models.py
import json
import tomllib
from typing import Any

from pydantic import field_validator

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel


class ServiceSettings(FormModel):
    name: str = Field(title='Service name', pattern=r'^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$')
    config: str = Field(
        '{\n  "replicas": 2\n}',
        title='Config (JSON)',
        ui_element='textarea',
        ui_options={'language': 'json', 'rows': 10},
    )
    build: str = Field(
        '[tool.build]\ntarget = "release"\n',
        title='Build settings (TOML)',
        ui_element='textarea',
        ui_options={'language': 'toml', 'rows': 6},
    )
    deploy_script: str = Field(
        '',
        title='Deploy script',
        ui_element='textarea',
        ui_options={'language': 'bash', 'code_highlight': False},
    )

    @field_validator('config')
    @classmethod
    def valid_json_object(cls, value: str) -> str:
        try:
            parsed: Any = json.loads(value)
        except json.JSONDecodeError as exc:
            raise ValueError(f'Not valid JSON: {exc.msg} (line {exc.lineno})') from None
        if not isinstance(parsed, dict):
            raise ValueError('The config must be a JSON object')
        return value

    @field_validator('build')
    @classmethod
    def valid_toml(cls, value: str) -> str:
        try:
            tomllib.loads(value)
        except tomllib.TOMLDecodeError as exc:
            raise ValueError(f'Not valid TOML: {exc}') from None
        return value
