Try submitting the form with a one-letter name: it comes back with "String should have at least 2 characters" under the name, and your email still filled in.

docs.title: validate()
docs.text:
SignupForm.validate() takes the raw request form, await request.form() in FastAPI or request.form in Flask, exactly as the framework gives it to you. There is nothing to convert first.

It returns a ValidationResult:

Attribute What it holds result.is_valid True when every field passed result.data The validated values as a dictionary, shaped like the model: {"name": "Ada", "email": "ada@example.com"} result.errors The error messages, keyed the same way: {"name": "String should have at least 2 characters"} result.render_with_errors() The form again, with the submitted values and the error messages

submit_url and any render options passed to validate() are remembered, so render_with_errors() needs no arguments. Use render_with_errors_async() in async routes.

docs.title: Showing submitted values safely
docs.text:
Anything the user typed is untrusted, even after it passes validation: validate() checks types and constraints, not whether a value is safe to put in HTML. Build HTML around submitted values with the library's html() function and a t-string (t"...", new in Python 3.14):

name = result.data["name"]
return html(t"<p>Thanks for signing up, {name}!</p>")

html() escapes every {value} in the t-string, so a name like <script>alert(1)</script> is shown as text, not run. An f-string or .format() would insert it as live HTML. This is the same mechanism the library uses for every piece of HTML it generates.

Next: Fields and Inputs.

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text:
Once a form has sub-forms, the same model can be shown as stacked sections, tabs, columns, collapsible panels or a step-by-step wizard. The model doesn't change: you pick the presentation with one layout= argument.

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel


class Contact(FormModel):
    email: str = Field(title='Email', ui_element='email')
    phone: str = Field('', title='Phone', ui_element='tel')


class Address(FormModel):
    street: str = Field(title='Street')
    city: str = Field(title='City')


class Preferences(FormModel):
    newsletter: bool = Field(False, title='Send me the newsletter')
    language: str = Field(
        'en', title='Language', ui_element='select', ui_options={'choices': ['en', 'fr', 'de']}
    )


class AccountForm(FormModel):
    model_config = {'title': 'About you'}

    name: str = Field(title='Full name')
    contact: Contact = Field(title='Contact details')
    address: Address = Field(title='Address')
    preferences: Preferences = Field(title='Preferences', ui_order=1)

Pass the layout both when rendering and when validating, so a failed submit comes back in the same layout:

FastAPIFlask 
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse
from models import AccountForm

from pydantic_schemaforms import html, render_form_html_async

app = FastAPI()
FORM_OPTIONS = {'layout': 'tabbed', 'include_framework_assets': True, 'asset_mode': 'cdn'}


@app.get('/account', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def show_account():
    return await render_form_html_async(AccountForm, submit_url='/account', **FORM_OPTIONS)


@app.post('/account', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def save_account(request: Request):
    result = AccountForm.validate(await request.form(), submit_url='/account', **FORM_OPTIONS)
    if not result.is_valid:
        return await result.render_with_errors_async()
    name = result.data['name']
    return html(t'<p>Saved {name}.</p>')

from flask import Flask, request
from models import AccountForm

from pydantic_schemaforms import html, render_form_html

app = Flask(__name__)
FORM_OPTIONS = {'layout': 'tabbed', 'include_framework_assets': True, 'asset_mode': 'cdn'}


@app.get('/account')
def show_account():
    return render_form_html(AccountForm, submit_url='/account', **FORM_OPTIONS)


@app.post('/account')
def save_account():
    result = AccountForm.validate(request.form, submit_url='/account', **FORM_OPTIONS)
    if not result.is_valid:
        return result.render_with_errors()
    name = result.data['name']
    return html(t'<p>Saved {name}.</p>')

docs.title: The layouts
docs.text:
layout= What you get "vertical" (default) The form's own fields first, then each sub-form as a titled section "tabbed" One tab for the form's own fields, then one tab per sub-form "accordion" The same groups as collapsible panels, the first one open "side-by-side" The same groups as columns in one row "wizard" The same groups as steps, one at a time, with Back and Next

Each sub-form, and each repeating sub-form, is one group. The grouped layouts need at least one sub-form; on a flat form they raise a ValueError telling you to split it into nested models.

After a failed submit, the first tab, panel or step that contains an error is the one that opens, and the error summary at the top stays visible.

docs.title: Group titles and order
docs.text:
• A sub-form's group is titled by its field's title ("Contact details").
  • The first group holds the form's own fields (here, the name). Its title is the model's title, model_config = {"title": "About you"}, or "General" when the model has none.
  • Groups follow the order the fields are declared in. ui_order changes it without moving code: ui_order=1 puts Preferences right after the first group.

docs.title: Wizard
docs.text:
layout="wizard" shows one group at a time with a progress header and Back and Next buttons; the submit button is on the last step.

from models import AccountForm

from pydantic_schemaforms import render_form_html

form_html = render_form_html(
    AccountForm,
    layout='wizard',
    wizard_options={'next_label': 'Continue', 'linear': True},
    submit_url='/account',
)
  • One form, one POST. All steps are in the same <form>, so the routes are exactly the ones above with layout="wizard". No state is kept between steps.
  • Next checks the current step with the browser's own validation (required, min, pattern, ...) and stays put if something is wrong. Pydantic still validates everything on submit.
  • Without JavaScript, every step is shown, stacked, with a normal submit button.

wizard_options sets the button labels, hides the progress header, or lets the header jump to any step ("linear": False). ui_step_title on a sub-form field gives its step a different title from its title. All the options are in the Layouts reference.

Layouts for content that isn't a form field

The library also has layout building blocks, such as a grid, tabs and cards, for arranging HTML you've already rendered. They're for page composition, not for forms; see Layout Primitives.

Next: Styling.

docs.title: Nested Forms and Lists
docs.text:
A bigger form is built from smaller ones. A field typed as another FormModel becomes a sub-form, and a field typed as a list of one becomes a repeating sub-form with Add and Remove buttons. There are no special classes to learn: it's ordinary Pydantic nesting.

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel


class Address(FormModel):
    street: str = Field(title='Street')
    city: str = Field(title='City', min_length=2)


class Pet(FormModel):
    name: str = Field(title='Name')
    age: int = Field(0, title='Age', ge=0)


class ProfileForm(FormModel):
    nickname: str = Field(title='Nickname')
    address: Address = Field(title='Home address')
    pets: list[Pet] = Field(
        default_factory=list,
        title='Pets',
        max_length=5,
        ui_add_button_label='Add a pet',
        ui_item_title_template='{name}',
    )

Use it with the routes from Handling Submissions. The form shows the nickname, then a "Home address" section, then a "Pets" list with an "Add a pet" button.

docs.title: Sub-forms
docs.text:
address: Address renders the Address fields as a titled section. The sub-form's own rules (min_length=2 on the city) apply as usual, and its fields can have their own sub-forms, as deep as you need.

Make a section collapsible with ui_collapsible=True, or start it collapsed with ui_collapsed=True (it opens by itself when it contains an error). An optional sub-form is typed Address | None.

docs.title: Repeating sub-forms
docs.text:
pets: list[Pet] renders one card per pet with Add and Remove buttons. Constraints count items: max_length=5 allows at most five pets, and min_length=1 would require at least one.

Setting Effect ui_add_button_label="Add a pet" Text of the Add button ui_item_title_template="{name}" Each card's title, filled from the item's fields; {index} is the 1-based position ui_collapsible_items=False Plain cards instead of collapsible ones ui_items_expanded=False Start the cards collapsed

docs.title: Data and errors are nested
docs.text:
validate() returns the data shaped exactly like the model:

{
    "nickname": "mk",
    "address": {"street": "1 Main", "city": "Paris"},
    "pets": [{"name": "Rex", "age": 3}, {"name": "Tux", "age": 1}],
}

and the errors shaped exactly like the data, so an error is found at the same path as its value:

{
    "address": {"city": "String should have at least 2 characters"},
    "pets": {1: {"age": "Must be 0 or greater"}},
}
  • A list's errors are keyed by the item's position, and only failing items appear.
  • A message about a whole list, such as too many pets, is a string at the list's key, or under "_errors" there when some items also have errors: {"pets": {"_errors": "...", 0: {...}}}.
  • result.error_list() gives the same errors as a flat list, [{"loc": ["pets", 1, "age"], "msg": "Must be 0 or greater"}], which is handy for logging and API responses.

When the form is re-rendered, each message appears next to its input and the summary at the top names the item: "Pet #2 — Age: Must be 0 or greater".

How the inputs are named

The inputs are named address.city and pets[0].name so the browser can submit them, and validate() decodes those names back into the nested data. You never need to build or parse them yourself, except when you post raw form data in a test.

Sub-forms are also what the grouped layouts arrange into tabs, columns, panels or wizard steps: that's the next chapter, Layouts.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
The same form renders for three styles. Pick one with framework=:

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel, render_form_html


class SignupForm(FormModel):
    name: str = Field(title='Full name')
    email: str = Field(title='Email', ui_element='email')


bootstrap_html = render_form_html(SignupForm, submit_url='/signup')
material_html = render_form_html(SignupForm, framework='material', submit_url='/signup')
plain_html = render_form_html(SignupForm, framework='none', submit_url='/signup')
Bootstrap (recommended)MaterialPlain HTML

The default. The form uses Bootstrap 5's classes (form-control, form-select, invalid-feedback, ...), so it matches the rest of a Bootstrap site, and validation states, icons and the grouped layouts use Bootstrap's components.

Your page loads Bootstrap. The form HTML contains the markup, not Bootstrap itself, so add Bootstrap's CSS and JS to your page template:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.0/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.0/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.js"></script>

The tutorial's include_framework_assets=True, asset_mode="cdn" adds these two tags to the form itself, which is handy for a page that has no template.

A Material Design 3 look with floating labels, built into the library: the form carries its own styles, so your page needs nothing extra and no Materialize or other CSS framework.

framework="none" gives clean, semantic HTML with no framework classes, ready for your own CSS.

Use the same framework= in validate() so a failed submit re-renders in the same style. The live demo can show any page in either style: add ?style=material to its address.

docs.title: Your own CSS
docs.text:
Every style keeps its markup predictable, so you can target it:

  • the <form> has the class pydantic-form (Material: md-form);
  • each input's id is its field name (email, address.city), and its help and error messages are <id>-help and <id>-error;
  • ui_class="..." and ui_style="..." on a Field() add a class or inline style to that field's input.
Forms with no external files

self_contained=True inlines all of Bootstrap, its icons and the library's scripts into the form HTML: no CDN, no static files. That's useful for an offline app, an intranet without internet access or a sandboxed iframe, but it adds several hundred kilobytes to every page. See Assets and Self-Contained Forms.

Next: CSRF Protection.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Validation is Pydantic validation: the rules live on the model, and validate() from Handling Submissions runs them. There are three levels, and you use them in this order:

  1. Constraints on Field() for a single value: length, range, pattern.
  2. @field_validator for a rule about one field that a constraint can't express.
  3. @model_validator for a rule about the form as a whole.
from datetime import date

from pydantic import ValidationInfo, field_validator, model_validator

from pydantic_schemaforms import Field, FormModel


class RegistrationForm(FormModel):
    username: str = Field(title='Username', min_length=3, max_length=20, pattern=r'^[a-z0-9_]+$')
    password: str = Field(title='Password', ui_element='password', min_length=8)
    confirm_password: str = Field(title='Confirm password', ui_element='password')
    age: int = Field(title='Age', ge=13, le=120)
    start_date: date = Field(title='Start date')
    end_date: date = Field(title='End date')

    @field_validator('username', mode='before')
    @classmethod
    def lowercase_username(cls, value: str) -> str:
        return value.strip().lower()

    @field_validator('confirm_password')
    @classmethod
    def passwords_match(cls, value: str, info: ValidationInfo) -> str:
        if value != info.data.get('password'):
            raise ValueError('Passwords do not match')
        return value

    @model_validator(mode='after')
    def end_after_start(self) -> 'RegistrationForm':
        if self.end_date < self.start_date:
            raise ValueError('The end date must be after the start date')
        return self

Use it with the routes from Handling Submissions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
Constraints are the first choice: they're one keyword, they're always checked on submit, and most of them also become HTML attributes, so the browser catches many mistakes before the form is even sent.

Constraint Checks Browser gets min_length=3, max_length=20 Length of a string or list minlength, maxlength pattern=r"^[a-z0-9_]+$" A regular expression pattern ge=13, le=120 At least / at most min, max gt=0, lt=100 Strictly greater / less than (checked on submit only) multiple_of=5 Divisible by (checked on submit only)

The messages are Pydantic's, with the range ones shortened: age=9 shows "Must be 13 or greater".

docs.title: Field validators
docs.text:
@field_validator is a classmethod that gets the value and returns it, possibly changed, or raises ValueError with the message to show.

Cleaning up a value is a mode="before" validator, so it runs before the constraints: lowercase_username turns " ADA " into "ada", which then passes the lowercase-only pattern.

Comparing with another field uses info.data, which holds the fields declared above this one that already passed. passwords_match puts its error on the confirmation field, right where the user needs to fix it.

docs.title: Model validators
docs.text:
@model_validator(mode="after") runs once every field has passed, with the whole form as self. Use it for rules that aren't about any single field. Its error is a form-wide error: it appears at the top of the form, in the error summary, as "Form: The end date must be after the start date", and in result.errors under the "_errors" key:

{"_errors": "The end date must be after the start date"}

A model validator only runs when every field is valid, so a user sees field errors first, then form-wide ones.

Field or form?

If the error has an obvious field to blame, use a field validator so the message sits next to that field. Use a model validator when it doesn't.

docs.title: Where errors show up
docs.text:
After a failed submit, result.render_with_errors() shows:

  • the user's values, still filled in;
  • each field's message under the field, with the field marked invalid for screen readers (aria-invalid) and linked to the message;
  • a summary at the top listing every error, including form-wide ones.

result.errors holds the same messages, shaped like the form: {"age": "Must be 13 or greater"}, and for sub-forms and lists, nested the same way as the data; see Nested Forms and Lists.

Rule-based validation and live validation

Pydantic validation covers almost every form. The library also has a rule-based layer (FormValidator, with ready-made rules such as EmailRule and PhoneRule) for rules you want to share between the submit route and live checks while the user types, or switch on and off per route. See Rule-Based Validation and Live Validation.
